purpose: NYC Results and Impact in Student Education (NYC RISE) with Adult Literacy Forward supports classes in English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL), Adult Basic Education (ABE), High School Equivalency (HSE), Basic Education in the Native Language (BENL), civics education, and digital literacy, as well as program supports and student services such as increased staff capacity, professional development, classroom infrastructure, contextualized curriculum and instruction, counseling and case management. Up to $100,000 of each award can be used for program enhancements and/or service expansion. Any amount above $100,000 must be used to provide new classes at a rate of $425 per instructional hour. Funding also supports NYC RISE data system and technical assistance provided by the Literacy Assistance Center.

legal_name: Agudath Israel of America Community Services, Inc.
purpose: This initiative supports organizations that work on a neighborhood level to combat the loss of affordable housing. Work includes, but is not limited to: tenant organization; code enforcement advocacy; housing court assistance, apartment repossession; and other housing-related public education. These efforts are informed by developing and executing neighborhood focused strategies, as well as providing demand driven services to individual residents. Support is also provided to enhance the capacity and technical skills of the providers within this initiative. Funding supports the Housing Preservation Initiative (HPI) which uses neighborhood based strategies that respond most effectively to various threats to affordable housing, and supports the Community Consultant Contracts (CCC) to provide general support and assistance to individuals seeking housing information, advice and referral services.

This initiative will strengthen the City’s immigration legal services by investing in coordination, direct services to low-income immigrants and technical support for immigration legal providers. Legal services to be provided include eligibility screenings, applications before USCIS such as for humanitarian relief and work authorization, motions before EOIR such as reopening cases, and changes in venue or hearing format, Special Immigrant Juvenile Status, detention support such as in-person or remote visits, petitions for habeas, and bond hearings, court accompaniment, rapid response legal assistance, wrap around services, and other pathways to secure legal immigration status, as impacted by need and demand. In addition, funding may be used to cover filing fees such as with USCIS, EOIR, and the BIA, legal research, costs to enhance data systems, outreach efforts, and emergency relief supplies such as public transit cards to attend court or emergency preparedness kits like in the event of a family member being detained. With prior approval from the City Council, a portion of the funding may also be used to subcontract with attorneys handling specialized immigration cases.

source: Immigration Legal Services for Survivors of Violence and Gender Based Harm
purpose: This Council-funded initiative will provide free immigration legal services to survivors of violence and gender-based harm in New York City. Services include direct legal representation, consultations, and assistance with applications for immigration relief, including U visas, T visas, asylum, family-based petitions, and other forms of protection. Services will be culturally and linguistically appropriate, trauma-informed, and accessible to diverse populations, prioritizing survivors who face heightened risk due to immigration status, gender, or safety concerns.

source: Know Your Rights for Immigrant Street Vendors
purpose: This initiative aims to create vendor-specific ‘Know Your Rights with immigration’ educational materials in seven different languages: Arabic, Bangla, French, Wolof, Spanish, Mandarin, and English. For Fiscal 2027, the non-profit organization will work with the Street Vendor Project to hold quarterly Know Your Rights workshops, run digital media campaigns to reach a wider audience of street vendors with Know Your Rights information on various social media platforms and will create multimedia content to distribute to vendors to increase accessibility for vendors with limited reading proficiency.

source: Language Access and Legal Services for Black Immigrants
purpose: This Council-funded initiative will remove barriers to interpretation and translation services for Black immigrant communities. Organizations funded under this initiative will support non-profit organizations seeking language services for their clients by directly providing the service and/or connecting them to professional interpreters and translators. Funding may be used to cover service fees and other operational expenses and provide culturally competency trainings to other community-based organizations. Participating providers will ensure that legal services and outreach materials are available and provided in their clients preferred.

Trauma recovery centers utilize multidisciplinary staff members that might include psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers and outreach workers to promote healing and break cycles of violence.

Services provided will include financial counseling and trainings, pre-purchase counseling, assistance with non-mortgage debt, loan modification and loss mitigation support (including the purchase of distressed mortgage notes), access to resiliency/repair programs, estate planning advice and workshops, drafting wills and other legal planning documents, deed theft assistance, legal assistance and counseling on clearing titles on homes where the legal ownership is not clear due lack of estate planning or other issues (tangled titles), litigation, referrals to other services to address liens and other encumbrances on tangled titles, research and advocacy around sub-prime lending and mortgage foreclosures, community outreach, and other related services.

Lastly, $168,000 will be allocated through DCLA to sponsor cultural performances and activities for veterans.
